title: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgvedic hotṛ priests: it explains the recitations of the Soma sacrifice, the Agnihotra and the royal consecration, with the dīkṣā as rebirth of the sacrificer as an embryo (1.3), the legend of Śunaḥśepa recited at the rājasūya (7.13–18), the derivation of the vyāhṛtis and Oṃ from Prajāpati's brooding (5.32), and the rites of kingship and the royal chaplain (book 8).

attribution.tradition: Mahidāsa Aitareya, son of Itarā (Sāyaṇa's introduction; ChU 3.16.7 names Mahidāsa Aitareya)
attribution.scholarly: a compilation of the Aitareyin school of the Ṛgveda; books 1–5 older than 6–8

scholarly.text: c. 800–600 BCE (older books earlier; estimates vary)

structure.description: 8 pañcikās of 5 adhyāyas each (40 adhyāyas), divided into khaṇḍas; cited pañcikā.khaṇḍa

title: Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) school of the Ṛgveda, explaining the fire-establishment, Agnihotra, new- and full-moon, seasonal and Soma rites from the hotṛ's side; it teaches that speech is the consecration and breath the consecrated (7.1) and that speech is spoken most distinctly in the north, where people go to learn it.
notes: The GRETIL e-text numbers the 'speech in the north' passage 7.7 (sentences 35–37); older citations give 7.6.

title: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Taittirīya school of the Black Yajurveda, supplementing the Saṃhitā's own prose: fire establishment, Agnihotra, Soma and royal rites, the nakṣatra offerings, the horse sacrifice, the cosmogony of Prajāpati diving as a boar to raise the earth (1.1.3), and the three Kāṭhaka chapters (3.10–12) on the Sāvitra, Nāciketa and Vaiśvasṛja fire-altars — including Naciketas' visit to Death (3.11.8), Bharadvāja's three lives of Vedic study (3.10.11) and the cosmic session of the world-creators (3.12.9).

attribution.tradition: the Taittirīya school, named after Tittiri (or, in the Purāṇic story, after the partridges (tittiri) who picked up the Yajus disgorged by Yājñavalkya)
attribution.scholarly: compiled within the Taittirīya school; the Kāṭhaka sections (3.10–12) derive from the Kaṭha school

structure.description: 3 aṣṭakas (kāṇḍas) of 8, 8 and 12 prapāṭhakas, divided into anuvākas

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina)
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of a hundred paths', the great Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda. It explains the whole Śrauta ritual — new- and full-moon, fire establishment, Agnihotra, ancestral offering, seasonal rites, Soma, royal consecration, the fire-altar (Agnicayana, books 6–10, with its 'secret' in book 10), horse, human and all-sacrifice, the funeral mound, the Pravargya — and teaches the sacrifice as the cosmic Person and year: Prajāpati fell apart after emitting creatures and is rebuilt in the altar. It records the teaching of Śāṇḍilya (10.6.3), the debates of Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court, the debts, the five great sacrifices, upanayana, Vedic self-study, the flood, and ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (14.4–9).

attribution.tradition: the White Yajus 'from the Sun' proclaimed by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya (ŚB 14.9.4.33 = BĀU 6.5.3)
attribution.scholarly: a compilation of the Vājasaneyin school; books 6–10 cite Śāṇḍilya as their authority, books 1–5 and 11–14 Yājñavalkya

scholarly.text: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; estimates vary)

structure.description: Mādhyandina recension: 14 kāṇḍas, 100 adhyāyas; cited kāṇḍa.adhyāya.brāhmaṇa.kaṇḍikā

notes: Commentaries: Harisvāmin (partial), Sāyaṇa. See also the Kāṇva recension (src:satapatha-brahmana-kanva).

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Kāṇva recension)
summary: The second recension of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, transmitted by the Kāṇva school of the White Yajurveda; its order of books differs from the Mādhyandina, and its last part is the Kāṇva Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the version on which Śaṅkara commented.
notes: Only partly edited in print for a long time; the Kāṇva BĀU is widely available.

title: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of twenty-five (chapters)' of the Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda: the chants (stotras and stomas) of the Soma sacrifices from one-day rites to year-long sessions, the Vrātya rites (17.1–4) by which outsiders are brought into the sacrificial community, the sessions along the Sarasvatī, and the teaching that Prajāpati alone was, with Speech as his own and his second, and that he released her to pervade all (20.14.2).

scholarly.text: c. 9th–7th c. BCE (among the older Brāhmaṇas; estimate)

title: Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa
summary: The 'twenty-sixth' chapter-book appended to the Pañcaviṃśa: rites of the Sāmaveda not covered there, sorcery and counter-sorcery rites, and in its final part (the Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa) the portents in the world — images of gods that laugh, weep or sweat, strange births and signs in the sky — with the propitiatory rites that avert them.

structure.description: 5 (or 6) prapāṭhakas; the last is the Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa

notes: Commentary: Sāyaṇa. Content of the Adbhuta section given from memory, chapter level.

title: Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The large Brāhmaṇa of the Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) Sāmaveda: an extended treatment of the Agnihotra (1.1–65), the year-long session and Soma rites, and many narratives, including Bhṛgu's journey through the other world where he sees the fruits of deeds (1.42–44) and the fate of the dead questioned at the gate of heaven.
notes: Known from South Indian manuscripts; the Jaiminīya school survives in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

title: Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa
summary: The 'secret' Brāhmaṇa of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda, functioning as that school's Āraṇyaka: meditations on the sāman chant, the udgītha, Oṃ and the breath (prāṇa), the journey of the dead through the sun, and a teacher lineage (vaṃśa); the Kena Upaniṣad forms part of its fourth book.

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas divided into anuvākas and khaṇḍas (numbering differs between editions)

notes: Correction to the task list: it is a Brāhmaṇa (an 'Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa'), not an Āraṇyaka in name, though it plays the Āraṇyaka's role for the Jaiminīyas. The Kena Upaniṣad is usually cited as JUB 4.18–21 (4.10 in Oertel's anuvāka numbering) — locator not verified here.

title: Jaiminīya Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Jaiminīya Sāmaveda list naming the seers (ṛṣi) of the sāman chants, so that each chant is sung with knowledge of its seer.

title: Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Kauthuma Sāmaveda manual of the application (vidhāna) of sāman chants outside the Soma ritual: expiations, protective and wish-fulfilling rites, and rites for gaining powers, each assigned a chant.

title: Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Kauthuma Sāmaveda index of the seers (ṛṣi) of the sāman chants; the tradition holds that one who uses a chant without knowing its seer, metre and deity gains no fruit.
notes: Local copy: vedaH/sAma/kauthumam/brAhmaNam (with Sāyaṇa's commentary, OCR).

title: Devatādhyāya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A short Sāmaveda text assigning deities to the sāman chants (and, by some accounts, colours to the metres).

title: Saṃhitopaniṣad Brāhmaṇa
summary: A short Sāmaveda text on the secret meaning of the continuous recitation (saṃhitā) of the chants and on the conditions for their proper transmission.

title: Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Sāmaveda list of the teachers through whom the Sāmaveda was handed down, traced back through the seers to Kaśyapa, the gods and Prajāpati, and finally to Brahman the self-existent.

title: Mantra Brāhmaṇa (Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa)
summary: The Kauthuma Sāmaveda collection of mantras for the domestic rites — marriage, conception, birth and the like — whose continuation (prapāṭhakas 3–10 of the 'Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa') is the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

title: Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
summary: The only surviving Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda. It opens with Brahman, the self-existent, alone in the beginning, who creates a second god from himself (1.1.1), tells of the origin of Atharvan and the Aṅgirases and of the Atharvaveda as the Veda of the brahman priest, discusses Oṃ at length, gives rules for the Vedic student, and in its later part explains Śrauta rites, often in words shared with other Brāhmaṇas.

scholarly.text: late; regarded as later than the major Brāhmaṇas, parts perhaps post-Pāṇinian

title: Kāṭhaka Brāhmaṇa (fragments)
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Kaṭha school of the Black Yajurveda, surviving in fragments and in the Kāṭhaka chapters taken into the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.10–12) and Āraṇyaka.

title: Vādhūla Anvākhyāna (Vādhūla Brāhmaṇa)
summary: Explanatory (Brāhmaṇa-type) narratives of the Vādhūla school of the Black Yajurveda, transmitted with its Śrautasūtra in Kerala manuscripts.
notes: Title and school from memory; content not summarized — gap for Phase C.

title: Śāṭyāyana Brāhmaṇa (lost)
summary: A lost Sāmaveda Brāhmaṇa of the Śāṭyāyanins, known only from quotations (e.g. in Sāyaṇa).

title: Aitareya Āraṇyaka
summary: The 'forest book' of the Aitareyins (Ṛgveda). Book 1 explains the Mahāvrata day; book 2.1–3 teaches the breath (prāṇa) as the recitation (uktha) and as the seers of the Ṛgveda, and the ascending clarity of the self in plants, animals and man (2.3.2); 2.4–6 is the Aitareya Upaniṣad; book 3 (Saṃhitopaniṣad) gives the secret meaning of continuous, word-by-word and step recitation; books 4–5 give the Mahānāmnī verses and the Mahāvrata in sūtra form.

structure.description: 5 āraṇyakas divided into adhyāyas and khaṇḍas

attribution.tradition: books 1–3 Mahidāsa Aitareya; book 4 Āśvalāyana and book 5 Śaunaka (Sāyaṇa)

notes: Commentary: Sāyaṇa; Śaṅkara on the Upaniṣad portion.

title: Kauṣītaki Āraṇyaka (Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka)
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Kauṣītaki/Śāṅkhāyana Ṛgveda: after chapters on the Mahāvrata it contains the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (adhyāyas 3–6, including Pratardana's 'inner Agnihotra', ŚĀ 4.5 = KU 2.5), a Saṃhitopaniṣad on recitation, the contest of the breath with the senses, an interiorized Agnihotra, and a closing teacher lineage.
notes: Order of chapters 7–15 given from memory at chapter level (low confidence).

title: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda: the Āruṇaketuka fire-altar (1); the book of Vedic self-study with the twilight worship, the wind-girdled seers who were śramaṇas (2.7) and the five great sacrifices (2.10); the cāturhotra altar (3); the Pravargya mantras and explanation (4–5); the funeral and ancestral mantras (6); the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (7–9); and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (10), which contains the mantras of the food-offering into the breaths.

structure.description: 10 prapāṭhakas (Āndhra recension; the Drāviḍa recension differs)

title: Kaṭha Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Kaṭha school of the Black Yajurveda, chiefly on the Pravargya rite, recovered from manuscripts.

title: Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
summary: The tenth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka: a collection of prayers and meditations (to Nārāyaṇa as the supreme, on truth, austerity and renunciation) that includes the mantras spoken when food is offered into the five breaths before a meal.
notes: Owned by U04 (minor Upaniṣads); entered here for the prāṇāgnihotra cross-reference.

title: Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Muktikā canon (attached to the Atharvaveda) teaching the 'sacrifice in the body' (śārīra-yajña): food eaten with mantras is offered into the breaths as into fires, and the parts and powers of the body and mind are identified with the priests, implements and fires of the sacrifice.
notes: Owned by U04; details of its correspondences not verified — see REPORT.
